questions.enonce_markdown: When from a given proposition another is derived having as its subjects the contradictory of the predicate of the original proposition, it is known as:

Select the most appropriate statement below;

*Options as printed:* A) All syllogisms are arguments, but not all arguments are syllogisms.   B) All syllogisms are inference, but not all inference are syllogisms.   C) Only inferences having two premises are syllogisms.   D) Only inferences having premises are syllogisms.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A syllogism is a deductive **argument**: two premises and a conclusion, with three terms. It is therefore a particular kind of argument, and many arguments (inductive arguments, arguments with one premise, arguments with more than two premises, arguments by analogy) are not syllogisms. Statement A says exactly this.

Statement B is also true in a loose sense, because a syllogism is a mediate inference and immediate inferences or inductions are inferences that are not syllogisms. It is less precise: "inference" names the mental process, "argument" names its expression in premises and conclusion. Statement C wrongly implies that any two-premise inference is a syllogism, and statement D is true of every inference, so it does not single out the syllogism.

**Intended answer: A (All syllogisms are arguments, but not all arguments are syllogisms).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which Fallacies are most clearly committed in the following syllogisms?

**i-** All p are M
All M are P
$\therefore$ All S are P

**ii-** No P and M
Some P are M
$\therefore$ Some S are not P

*Options as printed:* A) Exclusive premises and undistributed middle term.   B) Undistributed Middle Term and Exclusive premises.   C) Illicit process of the Minor Term, and Exclusive premises.   D) Illicit process of the Minor Term and Undistributed Middle Term.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The printed syllogisms are defective.** In (i) the minor term S appears only in the conclusion ("All p are M, All M are P" mention only P and M), and in (ii) "No P and M" and "Some P are M" again leave S out of the premises. As printed, neither argument is a three-term syllogism, so no option can be proved from the text.

The most probable intended forms are:

- (i) All P are M, All S are M, therefore All S are P (mood AAA in the second figure). The middle term M is the predicate of two affirmative premises, so it is **undistributed** in both. S is distributed in its premise ("All S are M"), so there is no illicit minor.
- (ii) No P are M, Some S are not M, therefore Some S are not P. Both premises are negative: **exclusive premises**.

Under that reading the fallacies are, in order, undistributed middle term and exclusive premises, which is option B (A states them in the reverse order; C and D name an illicit minor that does not occur).

**Probable intended answer: B (Undistributed Middle Term and Exclusive premises), assuming the corrected forms above.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following is FALSE?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The valid moods of the first figure are **AAA** (Barbara), **EAE** (Celarent), **AII** (Darii) and **EIO** (Ferio). The first figure requires a universal major premise and an affirmative minor premise.

- A: AAA and EAE are both valid: true.
- B: AAA and EIO are both valid: true.
- C: **AEE** has a negative minor premise, which the first figure forbids. In that figure the major term is undistributed in the affirmative major premise but distributed in the negative conclusion, an illicit process of the major term. AEE (Camestres) is valid only in the **second** figure. So the statement is FALSE.
- D: EAE and AII are both valid: true.

(These moods were tested by an exhaustive search over small models: AAA, EAE, AII and EIO hold in the first figure, while AEE fails there and holds in the second.)

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Moods AAA and EAE are valid in the first figure.
Moods AAA and EIO are valid in the first figure.
Moods AEE and EAE are valid in the first figure.
Moods EAE and A I I are valid in the first figure.

questions.enonce_markdown: The pure Hypothetical Syllogism is valid when the antecedent of the conclusion is the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A pure hypothetical syllogism has only conditional statements:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \supset q \quad \text{(major premise)} \\
q \supset r \quad \text{(minor premise)} \\
\therefore\ p \supset r
\end{array}
$$

The consequent of the major premise ($q$) is the antecedent of the minor premise: it is the middle term that disappears. The conclusion takes the antecedent of the **major** premise ($p$) as its antecedent and the consequent of the **minor** premise ($r$) as its consequent. The form was checked as valid with a truth table over the eight rows.

**Answer: A.**

C) The Simple Destructive Dilemma and Complex constructive Dilemma.   D) The Simple Destructive Dilemma and the Complex destructive Dilemma.

Classify the four dilemmas by the quality and the form of their conclusion:

| Complex constructive | affirmative, disjunctive ($r \vee s$) |

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following is clearly FALSE about Fallacies?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A fallacy is an error of **reasoning**: an argument that looks sound but is not, because it breaks a rule of logic. That is why textbooks call fallacies "counterfeit arguments" (A), "deceptive arguments" (B) and violations of logical rules (D; "roles" is a misprint in the paper).

"Mistaken beliefs" (C) is the false description: a false belief is a defect in the *content* of a proposition, while a fallacy is a defect in the *inference* from premises to conclusion. A person can hold a mistaken belief without having committed any fallacy, and a fallacious argument can even have true premises and a true conclusion.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select the Fallacy most clearly committed in the argument below: "terminally ill patient, have a right to doctor's assisted suicide after all, many of these people are unable to commit suicide by themselves"

Which fallacy is most clearly committed in the following argument "My experience with All Sailors I have done business with, shows that they are dishonest so it is clear to me that this Sailor is also dishonest"?

*Options as printed:* A) Fallacy of Accident.   B) Fallacy of converse accident.   C) Fallacy of Division.   D) Argumentum ad Populum.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The speaker starts from a general claim about sailors (built on his own limited dealings) and applies it to one more sailor without asking whether this man is an exception. Applying a general rule to an individual case to which it may not apply is the **fallacy of accident**.

The passage also contains a hasty generalisation (from the sailors met to sailors in general), which is the *converse accident*, so option B is a defensible description of the first step. Division (C) would need a property of a whole group or institution being passed to each of its members, and ad populum (D) appeals to the crowd, which is absent here.

**Intended answer: A (Fallacy of Accident).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these valid arguments forms inference is a Modus Ponens (MP)?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Modus Ponens (affirming the antecedent) has the form: a conditional, then the affirmation of its antecedent, therefore its consequent:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
p \supset q \\
p \\
\therefore\ q
\end{array}
$$

- A is exactly this form.
- B is two bare inferences ("$p$ therefore $q$", "$\sim p$ therefore $\sim q$") with no conditional premise at all.
- C is the **disjunctive syllogism** (valid, but not MP).
- D is the **pure hypothetical syllogism** (valid, but not MP).

(The validity of the four forms was checked with truth tables; only A has the shape of MP.)

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The statement; $(Y \supset \sim B) \cdot (B \cdot Y)$ can adequately be determined by the Truth Table as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Build the truth table (T = true, F = false):

| $Y$ | $B$ | $Y \supset \sim B$ | $B \cdot Y$ | $(Y \supset \sim B) \cdot (B \cdot Y)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | F | T | F |
| T | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | F | F |
| F | F | T | F | F |

The last column is false in **every** row, so the statement is a **contradiction** (self-contradictory). Intuitively: $B \cdot Y$ requires both $Y$ and $B$ to be true, but then $Y \supset \sim B$ is false. The table was recomputed with Python.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The "statement some politicians are dishonest" can best be translated into logical notation of propositional functions as
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $Px$ = "$x$ is a politician" and $Dx$ = "$x$ is dishonest". "Some politicians are dishonest" is an **I** proposition: there exists at least one individual who is a politician **and** dishonest.

$$
(\exists x)\,(Px \cdot Dx)
$$

- A is a universal conditional: "All politicians are dishonest" (an A proposition);
- C is a universal conditional with a negated consequent: "No politicians are dishonest" (an E proposition; the bracket is also unbalanced in the paper);
- D says "some politicians are *not* dishonest" (an O proposition).

Note that an existential statement uses a conjunction, not a conditional: $(\exists x)(Px \supset Dx)$ would be true as soon as something is not a politician.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: "Change in things is manifested in the process of separation" "Reality is characterized by the concept of performance, given that change is an absurdity" These two assertions are respectively attributed to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
- The first assertion is **Anaximander**'s: for him the boundless (the *apeiron*) gives rise to the world by the *separating out* of opposites (hot and cold, wet and dry). Thales explained things by water, and Anaximenes by air that thickens and thins (condensation and rarefaction), not by separation.
- The second assertion is **Parmenides**'s: Being is one, unchanging and permanent, and change is an illusion, an absurdity that thought cannot accept ("performance" in the paper is almost certainly a misprint for "permanence"). Zeno defended Parmenides with paradoxes against motion, but the thesis of permanence is the master's.

So the two assertions belong respectively to Anaximander and Parmenides.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these two paradoxes are used by Zeno to prove impossibility of motion?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Zeno of Elea defended Parmenides by four classic arguments against motion: the **Dichotomy (the racecourse)**, **Achilles and the tortoise**, the **Flying Arrow** and the **Stadium**. The Millet Seed (a falling seed makes no sound, yet the bushel does) is an argument about plurality and the senses, not about motion, so options A and B are wrong.

Option D lists two genuine motion paradoxes: the Arrow (at each instant the arrow occupies a space equal to itself, so it is at rest) and the Stadium. Option C mentions the racecourse, but "the relativity of motion" is not a standard name of one of Zeno's paradoxes (it is sometimes used to describe the Stadium), so D is the cleanest answer.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The Flying Arrow and the Millet Seed.
Achilles and tortoise and the Millet Seed.
The relativity of motion and racecourse.
The Flying Arrows and the Stadium.

questions.enonce_markdown: The maxim "Man is the measure of all things", was initially advanced by:
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Man is the measure of all things" is the best-known saying of the sophist **Protagoras**. It expresses relativism: what appears true to a person is true for that person. Gorgias is associated with nihilism (nothing exists, or cannot be known, or communicated), and Socrates opposed the relativism of the sophists by looking for universal definitions.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following are the best descriptions of Socrates dialectics?

*Options as printed:* A) Conversational and conceptual.   B) Contradiction and methodological doubt.   C) Critical and inductive.   D) Analytical and deductive.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Socratic dialectic is the art of **dialogue** (Greek *dialegesthai*, to converse): by questions and answers Socrates leads the other person to examine his opinions, and the search aims at the **concept**, the universal definition of virtue, justice, courage... That makes it conversational and conceptual (option A).

"Contradiction and methodological doubt" (B) is closer to Descartes. "Analytical and deductive" (D) does not fit a method that moves from particular examples to a definition. "Critical and inductive" (C) is also a defensible description, since the elenchus tests opinions and Aristotle credits Socrates with inductive arguments, which is why the question is ambiguous.

**Intended answer: A (Conversational and conceptual).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The process in Plato's Epistemology whereby the prisoner leaves the cave to attain indubitable knowledge is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Republic, the prisoner who is freed climbs out of the cave towards the light: from shadows and opinion to the sensible things, then to mathematical objects, and finally to the Forms and the Form of the Good. This upward movement of the intellect is Plato's **ascending dialectic**. The descending dialectic is the way back, from the Forms to their application. The *Allegory of the cave* (D) is the whole story, not the process; the turning of the soul (C) is only the first step of the ascent.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: According to Aristotle the power that a thing has to become something refers to
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Aristotle, change is explained by two states of being: **potentiality** (*dynamis*), the capacity of a thing to become something (the acorn is potentially an oak), and **actuality** (*energeia*), the realisation of that capacity (the oak). Change is the passage from potentiality to actuality, and entelechy names the fully achieved actuality.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these proofs of God's existence by Aquinas are based on the principle of Causality?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Aquinas's five ways are the proofs from (1) motion, (2) efficient cause, (3) contingency and necessity, (4) degrees of perfection and (5) the order (design) of the world. The first two are explicitly built on **causality**: everything that moves is moved by another, and nothing can be the efficient cause of itself, so a regress of movers or causes must stop at a first unmoved mover and first cause. Option B names exactly those two. Options A, C and D each pair one of them with a proof that rests on another principle (necessity, orderliness or perfection).

**Answer: B.**
themes: arguments for the existence of god

choix.texte: Proof from motion and efficient cause.
Proof from perfection and efficient cause.

questions.enonce_markdown: According to John Locke the origin of ideas is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Locke rejects innate ideas: the mind is a blank sheet (*tabula rasa*) and all our ideas come from **experience**. Experience has two sources, sensation (the outer senses) and reflection (the mind's inner observation of its own operations). "Sensation" (A) names only one of the two sources, so the origin of ideas as a whole is experience.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In an ascending order which of those sets adequately represents the Cartesian Rules of Methods

choix.texte: Clarity and distinction, analysis, synthesis, enumeration.
Enumeration, Clarity and distinctness, analysis, synthesis.
Analysis, Clarity and distinctness, enumeration, synthesis.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Marxist view that human existence is a class struggle between the Proletariat and the Bourgeoisie Classes is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Historical materialism** is Marx's theory that the material conditions of production determine social life and that history is the history of class struggle (masters and slaves, lords and serfs, bourgeoisie and proletariat). Dialectical materialism is the general philosophy of matter and of its contradictions (nature and thought), and "ideological materialism" is not a Marxist doctrine. The statement in the question is therefore historical materialism.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two of Peirce's methods of fixing beliefs that on one hand relate to man's relationship with God and on the other hand relates to man's attachment to his emotions and passions respectively are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In "The Fixation of Belief" Peirce names four methods: **tenacity** (clinging to what one already believes, out of habit and feeling), **authority** (belief imposed by an institution such as the state or the church, hence the link with religion and God), the **a priori** method (agreeableness to reason) and **science**.

"Respectively": the method tied to man's relationship with God is **authority**, and the method tied to man's attachment to his emotions and passions is **tenacity**. Option C gives them in that order. (The question is loosely worded: the first method is read through the church, the institution of religious authority.)

**Answer: C.**
themes: peirce and the fixation of belief

choix.texte: Method of tenacity and Method of Metaphysics.
Method of science and Method of Authority.
Method of Authority and Method of Tenacity.
Method of Tenacity and Method of science.

questions.enonce_markdown: Kierkegaard is generally considered a theistic existentialist because;
questions.corrige_markdown:
What makes Kierkegaard a *theistic* existentialist is that the answer he gives to anguish, despair and the "sickness unto death" is **faith in God**: the individual, through a personal leap of faith and a subjective commitment, relates himself to God. Options A, B and C describe his starting point (anguish, suffering, despair), which atheistic existentialists share; only D states the religious solution.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: He opines that philosophy must speak to anguished existence in an irrational world.
He considered the earth as a place of suffering, fear and dread.
He believes the central philosophical problem is sickness-unto-death.
It is only the subjective commitments to God that can grant relief.

questions.enonce_markdown:
By "abandonment" J.P. Sartre means that;

*Options as printed:* A) There is no common human nature or existence.   B) There is no ultimate reason why things are the way they are and not some other way.   C) Human beings are condemned to be free since there is no divine plan.   D) There is no objective standard of value for we are responsible for what we are.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In *Existentialism is a Humanism* Sartre uses "abandonment" (or forlornness) for the consequence of the non-existence of God: there is no *a priori* good and no value written in an intelligible heaven, so man is left alone, without excuses, and is responsible for what he is and for the values he chooses. That is option D.

Option C ("condemned to be free") is a closely related Sartrean idea and is also defensible; A refers to "existence precedes essence" and B to the absurd, so they do not define abandonment.

**Intended answer: D (There is no objective standard of value for we are responsible for what we are).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: This "apologetic" literature or in defense of an African way of thinking and seeing the world different from European way of seeing" is aptly qualified as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Ethnophilosophy** is the name given (notably by Hountondji, who criticised it) to the descriptive and apologetic literature that presents the collective world view of an African people as a philosophy, in defence of an African way of thinking different from the European one (Tempels's *Bantu Philosophy* is the model). "African philosophy" (D) is the broad field, and "pseudo-philosophy" (B) is a polemical label, not the usual name for this current.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following description is True of the relationship of forces and beings in Africa cosmogony:

*Options as printed:* A) It is hierarchical.   B) It is cyclic.   C) It is mutual.   D) It is interdependent.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the African world view described by Tempels and later by Mbiti, the universe is made of **forces** (vital forces), and beings are classified in an ordered scale: God, the ancestors, living humans, animals, plants and inanimate things. This **hierarchy of forces** is the best-known feature (option A). The same writers also stress that these forces influence one another, so that the whole is **interdependent** (option D), which is why the two options are both defensible.

**Best-supported answers: A (hierarchical) and D (interdependent); the printed key cannot be decided.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The notion of a "vital force" as foundational to the world view of all Bantu-speaking peoples of Eastern and Central Africa was advocated by:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Belgian missionary Placide **Tempels** presented "vital force" as the key of the Bantu world view and made being equivalent to force (*Bantu Philosophy*). Hountondji criticised that approach as ethnophilosophy, Odera Oruka is known for "sage philosophy", and Gyekye for work on communitarianism and the Akan.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The recognition of society as extension of the basic family unit; as an attitude of mind that reaches back to "tribal days" can aptly be qualified as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Ujamaa** ("familyhood" in Swahili) is Julius Nyerere's name for African socialism: the society is the extension of the basic family unit, a socialist attitude of mind that goes back to the traditional (tribal) community in which every member belonged, shared and worked for all. Consciencism is Nkrumah's philosophy, Pan-Africanism is the political movement for African unity, and "communalism" is a broader term that does not carry the "family extended to society" meaning of the question.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The view that, "our philosophy must find its weapons in the environment and living conditions of the African peoples", was basic of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence comes from Kwame **Nkrumah**'s *Consciencism*: African philosophy must start from the environment and the living conditions of the African peoples, so that it can serve their emancipation and the reconciliation of the traditional African, Islamic and Euro-Christian segments of their experience. Nyerere's Ujamaa and Senghor's Negritude have different starting points (the family model and the cultural identity of the black world).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these Meditations deals principally with the human mind?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Descartes's *Meditations*: the First is about the things that can be doubted, the **Second** about the nature of the human mind (the *cogito*, the self as a thinking thing, better known than the body), the Third about God and His existence, and the Fourth about truth and error. So the Second Meditation deals principally with the human mind.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these is the most correct order of the arguments used by Descartes to open all our knowledge to doubts?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the First Meditation Descartes first notes that the senses sometimes deceive, then uses the **dream argument** (waking and sleeping cannot be told apart by sure signs), then the hypothesis of an all-powerful **deceiving God** who could make him err even about the simplest truths, and finally replaces God by a malicious **evil demon** so as to doubt in a systematic way. The order is dream, deceiving God, evil demon.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: The dream, the deceiving God and the evil argument.
The deceiving God, the dream and the evil demon arguments.
The dream, the evil demon and the deceiving God arguments.
The evil demon, the dream and the deceiving God arguments.

questions.enonce_markdown: The purpose of the "Painter's Analogy" in The First Meditation is to show that:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Descartes compares the images of dreams to a painter's inventions: even the most fantastic creatures (sirens, satyrs) are composed from real elements (parts of animals, colours). He concludes that the sciences which study **composite things** (physics, astronomy, medicine) are doubtful, whereas the simplest and most general things (extension, shape, quantity, number: arithmetic and geometry) seem to remain certain. These simple notions fall only later, to the deceiving-God and evil-demon hypotheses. So the immediate purpose of the analogy is to show that the complex sciences are doubtful (C), not that simple and general knowledge is unreliable (D).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Paintings are drawn from real events.
Simple and general knowledge are unreliable.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of these is FALSE about Descartes' conception of man?

*Options as printed:* A) A man is a rational animal.   B) A man is being with the body and the soul.   C) A man is a thinking thing.   D) A man is a being that fears God.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Descartes man is a **thinking thing** (*res cogitans*) united with a body: a being made of soul (mind) and body (B and C are true). Descartes expressly **rejects the scholastic definition "rational animal"** in the Second Meditation because it leads to endless questions (what is an animal? what is rational?), so A is false as a statement about his conception.

Option D ("a being that fears God") is not a Cartesian definition of man either: Descartes does make man a creature dependent on God, but never defines him by the fear of God. That second doubtful option is why the question is ambiguous.

**Intended answer: A (A man is a rational animal).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which faculties according to Descartes, combined, are responsible for human error?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Fourth Meditation Descartes explains error by the concurrence of two faculties: the **understanding** (a limited power to perceive) and the **will** (an unlimited power to affirm or deny). Error arises when the will goes beyond the understanding and affirms what is not clearly and distinctly perceived. Neither the senses nor the imagination is the cause, so the combination is the will and the understanding (B).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
One theory of knowledge attributes all of human knowledge to a divine authority, while the other attributes it to human intelligence. This statement respectively refers to:

*Options as printed:* A) Empiricism.   B) Fideism.   C) Rationalism.   D) Empiricism and Fideism.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Fideism** holds that knowledge (above all of the highest truths) rests on faith and on divine authority. **Rationalism** holds that knowledge comes from human reason, the intelligence. The pair asked is therefore "Fideism and Rationalism", in this order. Empiricism makes experience (the senses) the source of knowledge, which is neither of the two theories described.

**No printed option gives the pair**: A and C name a single theory each, B (fideism) gives only the first member, and D pairs Empiricism with Fideism.

**Expected answer: Fideism and Rationalism (this pair is not among the printed options).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following 'principles of Aesthetic Appreciation' depict unity and brilliance?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the scholastic tradition (Aquinas), beauty requires wholeness or **completeness** (integrity, the unity of a thing that lacks nothing), proportion or **harmony**, and radiance or **splendor** (brilliance, clarity). "Unity" matches completeness and "brilliance" matches splendor, so the pair in the order of the question is "Completeness and splendor" (A). Option C lists the same two principles in the reverse order; B and D contain truthfulness, which is not one of the aesthetic principles.

**Answer: A.**
themes: aesthetics and the universality of beauty

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the pair that consists of Material and Spiritual culture respectively:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Material culture is made of the objects and techniques that can be touched (dress, tools, buildings, sculpture); spiritual (non-material) culture is made of beliefs, values, religion, language, music and songs. "Respectively" asks for a material element first and a spiritual one second: **dressing** (material) and **music** (spiritual), option A. B has two spiritual elements, C two material ones, and D reverses the order (songs, then sculpture).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Nietzsche's declaration that 'God is dead" most adequately implies that:

*Options as printed:* A) Humanity has been abandoned by God.   B) God does not exist.   C) God lacks the attributes of omnipotence.   D) Man should take his destiny in his hands.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For Nietzsche, "God is dead" is not a laboratory statement about a being but a diagnosis of European culture: belief in the Christian God, and with it the absolute values built on it, has lost its credibility. The consequence is that man can no longer rely on a transcendent source of meaning and must **create his own values and take his destiny in his own hands** (the theme of the overman). That is option D.

Option B ("God does not exist") is the literal reading, which is defensible but misses the point of the declaration; A is nearer to Sartre's abandonment; C does not correspond to anything Nietzsche says.

**Intended answer: D (Man should take his destiny in his hands).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: nietzsche and the death of god

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument that, any "attempt to show any disbelief in God entails self-contradiction" and the proofs of God's existence from motion, causation and contingency are generally considered as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The argument that denying God is self-contradictory is the **ontological argument** (Anselm: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived, so to deny that He exists is to contradict oneself). The proofs from motion, causation and contingency start from the existence of the world and move back to a first cause: they are **cosmological** (Aquinas's first three ways). The order asked is ontological, then cosmological (A); B reverses it, and the teleological argument is the one from design.

**Answer: A.**
themes: arguments for the existence of god

questions.enonce_markdown: The doctrine that holds that after death, the body and the soul will reunite and continue to live for eternity is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Resurrection** is the doctrine that after death the soul and the body are reunited and live for ever. The immortality of the soul (A) says only that the soul survives the death of the body, reincarnation (D) that the soul comes back in another body, and transfiguration (C) names a change of appearance, not the fate of the dead.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these theories of the origin of man have a negative implication on the morality of the society?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Creationism grounds morality in a creator to whom man answers, and pantheism and emanationism also link man to a divine principle. **Evolutionism**, read as saying that man is only the product of a blind struggle for survival, is the theory usually accused of weakening the basis of moral responsibility and of the dignity of the human person (B). The question reflects the textbook position; it is not a scientific claim about evolution.

**Answer: B.**
themes: theories of the origin of man

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is FALSE about the Principle of Double Effect?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The traditional conditions of the Principle of Double Effect are: (1) the act must be good, or at least indifferent, in itself (A); (2) the bad effect is foreseen but not intended; (3) the good effect must not be obtained **by means of** the bad effect (D); (4) there must be a grave (proportionate) reason to allow the bad effect (B).

Option C is not a condition: the principle says nothing about the act being an end in itself and not a means (many acts covered by the principle are means to a good end). So C is false.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The act must be good in itself.
There must be a grave reason for that act.
The act must be an end in itself not a means to an end.
The good must not be obtained by means of an evil act.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which three ethical principles and arguments below adequately militate in favour of the permissibility of violence?

*Options as printed:* A) Higher goods, and Sanctity of life   B) Sanctity of life and Double Effects and Malthusian Theory   C) Self Defence, Higher Goods and Slippery Slopes   D) Divine Command, Higher Good and Hippocratic Oath
questions.corrige_markdown:
Reasons usually given to justify violence are **self-defence** (protecting oneself and others) and the defence of **higher goods** (a greater good justifies a lesser harm). The slippery slope argument, by contrast, is normally used to *oppose* a permission (once violence is allowed it spreads), and the sanctity of life and the Hippocratic oath argue against taking life.

Every option mixes at least one principle that points the other way: A lists only two items and includes the sanctity of life; B includes the sanctity of life; C includes the slippery slope; D includes the Hippocratic oath. C has the two clearest pro-violence arguments (self-defence and higher goods) but is not strictly clean, so the question is unreliable.

**Closest option: C (Self Defence, Higher Goods and Slippery Slopes), although it is not strictly clean.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A system of centralized government in which only one party rules without opposition is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In **totalitarianism** the state is centralised and a single party controls political life and tolerates no opposition. Anarchy is the absence of government, an oligarchy is the rule of a small group, and a dictatorship is the rule of one person (or group) with absolute power, without necessarily the single-party organisation of the whole society. The best match for "only one party rules without opposition" is totalitarianism.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The theory of justice which advocates for equality for all men in the society is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **natural right (natural law) theory** holds that all men have by nature the same rights and the same dignity, which no law may take away, so justice demands equality for all. The social contract theory explains the origin of the state and of authority, the positive law theory identifies justice with the laws a state has actually enacted (which may be unequal), and the social good theory links justice to the common good.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
"The wages of sin is death" and give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God, what is God's"

*Options as printed:* A) Retributive justice and social justice.   B) Retributive justice and distributive Justice.   C) Retributive justice and commutative Justice.   D) Retributive justice and restorative justice.
questions.corrige_markdown:
"The wages of sin is death" is a punishment proportioned to the offence: **retributive justice**. The second quotation says that each party must be given what it is owed (taxes to the state, worship to God): rendering what is due is justice in the sense of giving each his due. Commutative justice (what individuals owe one another in exchanges, C) and distributive justice (what a community gives to its members, B) are both defensible readings; social justice (A) and restorative justice (D) fit less well.

**Best-supported answers: C (Commutative justice) or B (Distributive justice); the printed key cannot be decided.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The declaration of Karl Jaspers that "Philosophy is the courage to question the absolute" adequately implies that Philosophy is:

*Options as printed:* A) A Radical discipline.   B) A Radical discipline.   C) An Atheistic discipline.   D) A Critical discipline.
questions.corrige_markdown:
To question the absolute is to question even the foundations that are taken for granted, going to the root of things: philosophy is a **radical** discipline (it goes to the roots), and that radical questioning is also a **critical** attitude. Philosophy is not atheistic by definition (C): questioning the absolute does not mean denying it.

**The options are defective**: A and B are word for word identical ("A Radical discipline"), so a candidate cannot tell them apart, and D (critical) is also defensible.

**Intended answer: Philosophy is a radical (or critical) discipline; A and B are identical in print, so no single letter can be given.**
